question: Where is preventive and community nutrition counselling most likely to take place?

options.A: Schools and community health centers
options.B: Emergency surgery recovery rooms
options.C: Private hospital operating theatres
options.D: Intensive care units in large hospitals

explanation: Community and preventive efforts happen where everyday people live, work, and study, such as schools and local clinics. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T002#GNS227_U7_T002_h5)

question: A patient with a bleeding disorder needs a blood sample drawn. As a nurse, what is your best action?

options.A: Apply prolonged direct pressure to the venipuncture site after removing the needle
options.B: Massage the puncture site vigorously immediately after pulling out the needle
options.C: Apply a cold ice pack to the arm for thirty minutes before attempting the draw
options.D: Use the largest gauge needle available to speed up the blood collection process

explanation: Because their blood takes longer to form a plug, holding firm, direct pressure on the needle site for an extra-long time prevents large, painful bruises (hematomas).

question: What is the primary goal of nursing interventions in family-centered care?

options.A: To make all healthcare decisions on behalf of the household head
options.B: To strengthen the family's ability to care for its members independently
options.C: To permanently remove sick family members into institutions
options.D: To eliminate the need for doctors

explanation: Good nursing support empowers families so they gain confidence to manage their health challenges over time.

question: Under which category of supplements is iron classified?

options.A: Enzyme
options.B: Vitamin
options.C: Mineral
options.D: Herb

explanation: Iron is a vital mineral our bodies need to build hemoglobin for red blood cells. Simple and classic nursing knowledge!

question: What do we call the layer of a membrane that is stuck directly onto the surface of an organ?

options.A: parietal layer
options.B: visceral layer
options.C: mucosal layer
options.D: fibrous layer

explanation: Remember: 'visceral' relates to the internal organs themselves, while 'parietal' lines the outer wall of the cavity.

question: When starting a 'less than' ogive on graph paper, where should your very first point land on the x-axis?

options.A: At the highest possible number recorded in the entire study
options.B: Right in the middle of the very last group listed
options.C: At the exact median value calculated for the sample
options.D: At the lower boundary of the first class where frequency is zero

explanation: That's it! We anchor our 'less than' ogive right at the starting line—the lower boundary of the first class where no data has piled up yet.

question: Which human infectious disease is the only one successfully eradicated globally so far?

options.A: Tuberculosis
options.B: Malaria
options.C: Measles
options.D: Smallpox

explanation: Correct! Through a massive worldwide vaccination campaign led by the WHO, smallpox was completely wiped out.

question: What is the primary biological reason for the physical changes women feel during perimenopause?

options.A: Permanent closure of the cervical canal
options.B: Gradual depletion and decreased responsiveness of ovarian follicles
options.C: Complete failure of the anterior pituitary gland
options.D: Sudden permanent stoppage of all thyroid hormones

explanation: As the ovaries naturally run low on active egg follicles, estrogen and progesterone levels start rollercoasting before settling down.

question: What two structures combine to form the striatum?

options.A: Caudate nucleus and putamen
options.B: Putamen and globus pallidus
options.C: Caudate nucleus and substantia nigra
options.D: Thalamus and subthalamic nucleus

explanation: The caudate nucleus and the putamen together make up the striatum, which is the main receiving area for inputs coming into the basal ganglia from the cerebral cortex. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T12#GNS211_U3_T12_h1)

question: Why should a nurse avoid using household kitchen spoons to measure liquid medications?

options.A: Using them makes the liquid spill on the table
options.B: Household spoons react chemically with liquid drugs
options.C: Kitchen spoons are too heavy for patients to hold
options.D: Kitchen spoons vary in size and give inaccurate doses

explanation: Household spoons are not standardized for medical measurements, which can lead to giving too much or too little medicine. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h4)

question: Where is the insular lobe located within the brain?

options.A: At the very back of the skull
options.B: Deep inside the lateral sulcus
options.C: Right behind the forehead bones
options.D: On the outer surface of the temples

explanation: The insula is buried deep within the lateral sulcus, hidden beneath the other overlying lobes. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T23#GNS211_U3_T23_h6)

question: In parasitism, what best describes the relationship between the parasite and its host?

options.A: Both organisms benefit equally from the interaction
options.B: The host benefits while the parasite remains unaffected
options.C: Both organisms suffer damage from living together
options.D: The parasite benefits while harming the host

explanation: You've got this! In parasitism, the parasite takes what it needs to survive (like nutrients and shelter) at the expense of the host. Think of it as a one-sided relationship where the guest hurts the home.

question: What physical feature of capillaries makes the exchange of substances possible?

options.A: Walls that are only one cell thick
options.B: Direct connections to large veins
options.C: Valves that stop blood from flowing backward
options.D: Thick muscular layers that pulse strongly

explanation: The ultra-thin single-cell wall of a capillary allows easy diffusion of gases and nutrients between blood and tissue cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h4)

question: Which activity is an effective way to reach a large group of people during a community mental health campaign?

options.A: Market square talks and radio awareness programs
options.B: Locking patients inside a quiet room
options.C: Destroying traditional medicine books
options.D: Waiting quietly at the clinic for someone to walk in

explanation: Reaching out through public spaces and mass media ensures that mental health messages reach everyday community members where they gather. [learn more](GNS314_U4_T7#GNS314_U4_T7_h7)

question: Why must cold chain costs be included when calculating logistics for vaccines?

options.A: Refrigeration equipment requires ongoing power and servicing to keep products potent
options.B: Keeping vaccines cold increases their weight and doubles the shipping fees
options.C: Cold storage fees are paid directly to the patients who receive the vaccines
options.D: Government regulations prohibit charging patients for unrefrigerated medicines

explanation: Vaccines need steady refrigeration to stay active. Maintaining fuel and power adds real financial costs to the supply chain!

question: Which common infrastructure problem makes it hard to store medications like insulin in patient homes?

options.A: Unreliable electricity grids
options.B: Frequent fuel price increases
options.C: Poor telecommunication networks
options.D: Inadequate road construction

explanation: Well done! Drugs that need a fridge, like insulin, struggle when power supply is erratic.

question: What is the main purpose of doing a baseline psychiatric assessment for a patient with a degenerative illness?

options.A: To diagnose the exact genetic mutation causing the disease
options.B: To establish a baseline for the patient's mood and cognitive status
options.C: To replace the need for a physical neurological examination
options.D: To test the patient's physical strength and balance

explanation: Taking a baseline measurement lets us see where the patient stands today, so we can track any mental or emotional changes later on.

question: What is the main goal of doing a home visit when assessing family vulnerability?

options.A: To search the house for stolen property
options.B: To check out environmental hazards and living conditions firsthand
options.C: To collect local government taxes from the residents
options.D: To force the family to sweep their yard immediately

explanation: Brilliant! Visiting a home lets you see real-life conditions—like how they store drinking water—that they might not mention during a clinic chat.

question: Why do state or regional health schemes often exist alongside a national scheme?

options.A: To address local health priorities and specific regional demographics
options.B: To compete directly with private international clinics
options.C: To prevent rural residents from visiting city hospitals
options.D: To collect extra taxes without government approval

explanation: Correct! State schemes let local governments customize health packages to fit the unique cultural and financial needs of their own people.

question: What is the main job of emergency contraception?

options.A: To terminate an established pregnancy safely
options.B: To serve as a regular daily family planning method
options.C: To prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse
options.D: To protect against sexually transmitted infections

explanation: Think of emergency contraception as your backup plan after a contraceptive slip-up or unprotected sex. It is not meant for daily family planning and doesn't work if a pregnancy has already started. You've got this!

question: When should a nurse researcher use the median instead of the mean?

options.A: When the data contains extreme outliers or is heavily skewed
options.B: When every single data point needs to be included in the calculation
options.C: When working exclusively with large, perfectly symmetrical bell curves
options.D: When the data represents simple categorical groups with no numbers

explanation: The median ignores extreme highs and lows, giving you a much truer picture of the center when your data is lopsided.

question: What common farming practice greatly increases the spread of Taenia solium in rural areas?

options.A: Keeping pigs strictly indoors in concrete pens with automated cleaning
options.B: Free-range scavenging of pigs where human waste is accessible
options.C: Vaccinating all livestock against bacterial infections yearly
options.D: Feeding cattle exclusively on imported commercial grain

explanation: That's right! When pigs roam about freely and have access to human faeces where open defecation occurs, they easily pick up tapeworm eggs.

question: What is the standard temperature range for storing most routine vaccines in a clinic fridge?

options.A: Minus 20 degrees Celsius to minus 10 degrees Celsius
options.B: Minus 5 degrees Celsius to zero degrees Celsius
options.C: Plus 2 degrees Celsius to plus 8 degrees Celsius
options.D: Plus 15 degrees Celsius to plus 25 degrees Celsius

explanation: Commit +2°C to +8°C to memory! As a nurse managing the cold chain in your clinic, this is your golden rule for keeping vaccines potent.

question: A home care nurse is helping a diabetic patient manage blood sugar using local Nigerian foods. What is the best approach?

options.A: Insist the patient only eat imported foods recommended in standard textbooks
options.B: Tell the patient to stop eating altogether until blood sugar normalizes
options.C: Ignore the diabetes and let the patient eat whatever they want
options.D: Adapt the diabetic meal plan using accessible local staples and traditional foods

explanation: Brilliant! Good nursing means working with familiar, local foods so the patient can easily stick to their health plan.

question: Why is addiction considered a chronic brain disease instead of just a lack of willpower?

options.A: It permanently alters brain circuits related to reward and self-control
options.B: It only affects people with inherited genetic weaknesses in their lungs
options.C: It completely stops the liver from producing digestive enzymes
options.D: It causes immediate physical paralysis in every single user

explanation: Think of it this way: long-term substance use physically changes how the brain's wiring works, making self-control super difficult without proper support. It's a health condition, not a character flaw!

question: Why must a good management plan have a broad scope?

options.A: To eliminate the need for inter-departmental communication
options.B: To anticipate how changes in one department affect other units
options.C: To make the planning document look impressive to inspectors
options.D: To ensure every single employee works overtime every week

explanation: Hospital units are closely connected. A comprehensive plan looks at the entire system rather than isolating just one ward.

question: Why does the tissue lining the urethra change from transitional cells near the bladder to tough squamous cells near the opening?

options.A: Different tissues are required to filter bacteria out of the urine stream.
options.B: The external opening needs tougher tissue to protect against friction and environmental exposure.
options.C: The cells near the outside must produce mucus to lubricate the reproductive tract.
options.D: Changes in urine acidity destroy transitional cells as the fluid travels downward.

explanation: Makes total sense, right? Tough squamous cells protect the outer opening from daily wear and tear.

question: What is the main job of our everyday eccrine sweat glands?

options.A: Thermoregulation
options.B: Secreting earwax
options.C: Producing body odor
options.D: Waterproofing the hair

explanation: You got it! Eccrine glands release water onto our skin, cooling us down as it evaporates when our body temperature rises.

question: According to the WHO, what BMI range is considered a normal, healthy weight for an adult?
explanation: Correct! A BMI between 18.5 and 24.9 is the sweet spot classified as normal weight by the World Health Organization.

question: The main benefit of assertive communication for patient safety is that it...

options.A: speeds up the hospital discharge process completely
options.B: replaces the need for doctors to write prescriptions
options.C: stops unsafe orders from being carried out blindly
options.D: ensures patients never experience hospital side effects

explanation: An assertive nurse speaks up immediately when a care plan poses a risk to the patient. [learn more](GST321_U7_T5#GST321_U7_T5_h3)

question: A patient diagnosed with active Lassa fever is admitted to a special ward. What infection control action is this?

options.A: Isolation
options.B: Surveillance
options.C: Immunization
options.D: Quarantine

explanation: Separating a person who already has an active disease diagnosis is classified as isolation. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T5#GNS313_U2_T5_h2)

question: A nurse is accidentally poked by a needle from a patient who has Hepatitis B. Why is this exposure especially scary?

options.A: Hepatitis B spreads easily through casual air contact in the room.
options.B: There are no post-exposure vaccines or treatments available for Hepatitis B.
options.C: Hepatitis B has the highest transmission risk per exposure among common bloodborne viruses.
options.D: Hepatitis B can instantly destroy human skin cells on contact.

explanation: Compared to HIV or Hepatitis C, Hepatitis B is much more infectious. A single contaminated prick has a very high chance of passing the virus on if you aren't vaccinated.

question: Which type of illness spreads the fastest in crowded, poorly sanitized relief camps?

options.A: Degenerative joint diseases
options.B: Chronic autoimmune conditions
options.C: Waterborne infectious diseases
options.D: Hereditary metabolic disorders

explanation: Spot on! When clean water and toilets break down, infections like cholera and dysentery spread through the camp like wildfire.

question: What natural materials are most commonly used to make traditional herbal remedies?

options.A: Sterile surgical instruments
options.B: Processed industrial plastics
options.C: Synthetic chemical tablets
options.D: Roots, barks, and leaves

explanation: Easy peasy! Traditional healers prepare various remedies directly from local plants, utilizing roots, barks, and leaves.

question: A patient's forehead temperature reads 37.8°C, but they look pale and are shivering hard. What should you suspect?

options.A: The patient has a severe brain injury
options.B: Shivering can make skin feel cold while a real fever is hiding underneath
options.C: The thermometer is definitely broken and should be thrown away
options.D: The patient has no fever at all and needs no more checks

explanation: When shivering causes surface blood vessels to tighten up, skin readings can look normal or low even when core temperature is climbing. Always keep a close eye!

question: Which part of a feedback loop is responsible for detecting a change in the body?

options.A: Set point
options.B: Receptor
options.C: Effector
options.D: Control center

explanation: Spot on! Receptors act as your body's scouts or sensors, picking up any changes (stimuli) in your internal or external environment.

question: What is the usual waiting time between taking mifepristone and taking misoprostol?

options.A: 5 to 7 days
options.B: 2 weeks
options.C: 24 to 48 hours
options.D: 1 to 2 hours

explanation: Spot on! Patients usually wait 24 to 48 hours after swallowing the mifepristone tablet before taking the misoprostol.

question: What does the ethical principle of non-maleficence require of a nurse?

options.A: To let clients make every medical decision independently
options.B: To divide hospital resources equally among all available staff
options.C: To do no harm and protect the client from injury
options.D: To always tell the absolute truth regardless of consequences

explanation: Non-maleficence is the core professional duty to avoid inflicting physical or emotional harm on the client. [learn more](GST321_U10_T5#GST321_U10_T5_h2)

question: How should a nurse collect a urine sample from a patient with a catheter?

options.A: By disconnecting the catheter tubing from the drainage bag
options.B: From the rubber sampling port using a sterile syringe
options.C: By squeezing urine backward from the tubing into the bladder
options.D: From the bottom valve of the plastic collection bag

explanation: Always use the special needleless sampling port with a sterile syringe. Never take urine from the drainage bag, as those germs have been sitting there and won't give an accurate lab result!

question: What is a dual-chamber pacemaker designed to do?

options.A: Pace both an atrium and a ventricle
options.B: Store two separate batteries for emergencies
options.C: Pace the left and right lungs together
options.D: Monitor blood pressure and breathing rate

explanation: A dual-chamber system uses two leads to coordinate contractions in both upper and lower chambers of the heart. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T9#GNS321_U2_T9_h2)

question: Why must nurses remind patients never to stop taking their antidepressants all of a sudden?

options.A: Abrupt discontinuation instantly cures the chemical imbalance
options.B: Stopping quickly causes immediate permanent brain damage
options.C: Sudden cessation can trigger withdrawal symptoms and a return of depression
options.D: Patients will develop a physical addiction to the medication

explanation: Spot on! Stopping suddenly can cause uncomfortable withdrawal effects and bring the depression rushing back. Medication always needs to be tapered off safely under medical guidance.

question: Why should hospitals use fixed routes and specific schedules for moving waste carts through corridors?

options.A: To keep waste moving during quiet times and avoid crowds
options.B: To allow doctors to examine the waste on its way out
options.C: To give transport staff regular exercise breaks
options.D: To ensure waste carts pass every patient bed for inspection

explanation: Transporting waste when hallways are busy increases the risk of collisions, spills, and public exposure to hazardous materials. [learn more](GST114_U6_T12#GST114_U6_T12_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of injection safety in nursing practice?

options.A: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing medical supplies
options.B: To ensure injections do no harm to the patient or worker
options.C: To speed up the administration of routine vaccinations
options.D: To eliminate the need for personal protective equipment

explanation: Injection safety focuses entirely on protecting patients, healthcare workers, and the community from injury and disease transmission during injection procedures. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h1)

question: Why do healthcare facilities use incident reports?

options.A: To calculate the patient's final hospital expenses
options.B: To improve safety and prevent future occurrences
options.C: To provide permanent legal evidence inside patient charts
options.D: To find which specific nurse to blame for a mistake

explanation: That is right! Incident reports help hospitals catch system hazards so they can fix policies and protect future patients.

question: Why is training local mothers as peer educators so effective in stopping harmful food taboos?

options.A: Mothers are legally required by the state to teach nutrition classes
options.B: Peer educators have advanced university degrees in clinical medicine
options.C: Mothers listen to fellow community peers who share similar daily life experiences
options.D: Peer educators receive a high monthly salary from international donors

explanation: People are much more likely to adopt new health habits when taught by trusted neighbors from their own background rather than outsiders.

question: Why is obtaining a baseline physical assessment during admission important?

options.A: It gives you a standard to compare future health changes against
options.B: It allows the nurse to discharge the patient much faster
options.C: It guarantees the patient will not develop new complications
options.D: It prevents the patient from asking questions about their care

explanation: Initial baseline data lets the nurse spot subtle improvements or sudden declines during the hospital stay. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h1)

question: What does a 'narrow therapeutic index' tell a nurse about a medication?

options.A: The safety margin between healing and toxicity is small
options.B: The drug requires a very large dose to work properly
options.C: The body metabolizes the drug extremely quickly
options.D: The medicine has high potency and long half-life

explanation: Think of this like walking a tightrope: the dose that heals and the dose that harms are very close to each other, so we must monitor the patient closely!

question: What is the primary benefit of herd immunity in a community?

options.A: It replaces the need for personal hygiene and clean water
options.B: It completely eliminates all viruses from the global environment
options.C: It protects vulnerable individuals who cannot receive vaccines
options.D: It guarantees that natural infections never occur again

explanation: When enough people are immune, the chain of infection breaks, offering indirect protection to vulnerable, unvaccinated people. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which body problem is a very common cause of sudden confusion or unconsciousness?

options.A: Severe hypoglycemia
options.B: A ruptured cerebral aneurysm
options.C: Bacterial meningitis
options.D: A penetrating skull fracture

explanation: Spot on! When blood sugar drops too low (hypoglycemia), the brain gets starved of its main energy source and shuts down fast.

question: What is the main difference between tertiary and secondary healthcare?

options.A: Tertiary care involves highly specialized sub-specialists and advanced technology
options.B: Tertiary care is located in every small rural village across the country
options.C: Secondary care requires medical students for operation, unlike tertiary care
options.D: Secondary care handles complex brain surgery while tertiary care handles basic immunization

explanation: When cases get super complex, they go to tertiary centers. They have advanced technology and sub-specialists that standard general hospitals don't usually have.

question: What is the main job of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)?

options.A: It breaks down stored fat to generate body heat and energy.
options.B: It prevents the hypothalamus from releasing thyrotropin-releasing hormone.
options.C: It signals the thyroid gland to produce and release thyroid hormones.
options.D: It directly lowers high blood calcium levels in the bloodstream.

explanation: You got it! TSH is released by the pituitary gland to tell the thyroid when it's time to make and pump out more hormones.

question: How does a fear of blame usually affect a nurse's problem-solving ability?

options.A: It improves the nurse's analytical and critical thinking skills
options.B: It encourages the nurse to report errors immediately
options.C: It causes the nurse to hide mistakes instead of fixing them
options.D: It helps the healthcare team work faster during emergencies

explanation: When people fear punishment, they tend to conceal errors rather than addressing the root problem openly. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h5)

question: A student with asthma starts wheezing badly during sports. What should the school nurse do first?

options.A: Send the student home immediately without any medical assessment
options.B: Tell the student to run faster to clear their airways naturally
options.C: Assess the student and administer the prescribed rescue inhaler
options.D: Wait until the end of the school day to notify the parents

explanation: You got it! The nurse needs to quickly check the student and give their emergency rescue inhaler as outlined in their care plan.

question: What is a strict safety rule for a patient being discharged after receiving sedation for an endoscopy?

options.A: They must have a responsible adult escort to take them home.
options.B: They must sign a new consent form before leaving the clinic.
options.C: They must stay in the hospital ward for at least three days.
options.D: They must avoid eating solid food for an entire week.

explanation: Because sedatives stay in the system for hours, patients are not allowed to go home alone or drive themselves. They need a trusted companion!

question: Why can a normal blood pressure reading sometimes be misleading in early cardiovascular shock?

options.A: Only the pulse rate matters during a cardiac crisis
options.B: Heart conditions never affect blood pressure numbers
options.C: The body's compensation keeps pressure normal before it crashes
options.D: Blood pressure cuffs are notoriously inaccurate in emergency rooms

explanation: The body works hard to keep blood pressure stable by narrowing blood vessels, meaning the patient can suddenly crash later. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h4)

question: What is NOT a typical activity managed through nursing research informatics?

options.A: Managing large health datasets and clinical trial records
options.B: Storing digital archives of peer-reviewed clinical literature
options.C: Calculating monthly salary disbursements for hospital employees
options.D: Analyzing statistical outcomes of evidence-based nursing studies

explanation: Salary calculations are an administrative task, whereas research informatics focuses on scientific studies, data analysis, and literature management. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T2#GNS113_U1_T2_h5)

question: Immediately after a natural disaster, what is a top health priority for teams like the WHO?

options.A: Issuing passports to displaced citizens
options.B: Managing international commercial trade agreements
options.C: Designing long-term economic policies for the affected country
options.D: Preventing secondary health crises like waterborne disease outbreaks

explanation: Well done! When clean water systems break down, diseases like cholera can spread fast, so stopping secondary outbreaks is a top priority.

question: What actually happens when a patient experiences hormone resistance?

options.A: Target cell receptors fail to respond to normal hormone levels
options.B: The pituitary gland blocks the bloodstream to the target tissue
options.C: The liver destroys circulating hormones before they reach organs
options.D: The endocrine gland completely stops producing all chemical messengers

explanation: Imagine knocking on a door (the hormone), but the doorbell is broken so nobody answers (the cell receptor). The hormone is present in the blood, but the cells just won't listen to it!

question: A nurse notices women in a village prefer risky home births due to tradition. What is the best first step?

options.A: Report all pregnant women in the village to the local police
options.B: Provide culturally sensitive education and build trust regarding hospital delivery benefits
options.C: Refuse to treat any woman who has previously given birth at home
options.D: Ignore the practice since culture cannot be influenced by health workers

explanation: Yarn true! Respecting people's culture while gently building trust is the best way to help them see the safety of hospital deliveries. [learn more](GNS216_U1_T6#GNS216_U1_T6_h6)

question: Why do we break long-term rehab down into small, bite-sized goals?

options.A: They eliminate the need for any further nursing assessments
options.B: They guarantee that the patient will be discharged within forty-eight hours
options.C: They ensure the insurance company approves unlimited hospital stays
options.D: They prevent client frustration and help maintain motivation during a long recovery

explanation: Recovery can feel overwhelming. Small daily wins keep patients motivated and smiling instead of giving up. You're doing great!

question: What do we call a sudden, involuntary spasm of the vocal cords that blocks a patient's airway?

options.A: Bronchial asthma
options.B: Pleural effusion
options.C: Pulmonary embolism
options.D: Laryngospasm

explanation: Brilliant! A laryngospasm is when the vocal cords suddenly clamp shut, making it hard to breathe and needing quick action.

question: What is the main characteristic of individuals placed in quarantine?

options.A: They have no symptoms yet
options.B: They are completely immune to the disease
options.C: They show clear symptoms of illness
options.D: They refuse medical treatment

explanation: Quarantine is strictly for healthy people who were exposed to a disease so we can watch if they get sick. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h1)

question: How does team nursing differ from total patient care?

options.A: Total patient care involves no registered nurses at all
options.B: Total patient care is only used in surgical operating theatres
options.C: Team nursing uses a mix of different staff cadres to care for a group of patients
options.D: Team nursing requires one registered nurse to do everything alone

explanation: Well done! Total patient care means one nurse handles everything for a patient, while team nursing shares the workload among a group of mixed staff.

question: What actually defines an ethical dilemma in nursing?

options.A: A situation where two or more moral principles conflict with each other
options.B: A disagreement between a nurse and a doctor over medication dosage
options.C: A patient refusing to pay their nursing agency bills
options.D: A broken piece of medical equipment inside the patient's home

explanation: Spot on! It's a tough spot where every choice seems to break a moral rule, and there is no easy right or wrong answer.

question: When checking lab results, which finding usually tells you the patient's body is actively fighting off an infection?

options.A: Low platelet concentration levels
options.B: Reduced blood urea nitrogen
options.C: Elevated white blood cell count
options.D: Decreased red blood cell count

explanation: You got it! A high white blood cell count (leukocytosis) means the bone marrow is pumping out extra soldiers to tackle invading germs.

question: What is typically one of the earliest physical signs of significant blood loss?

options.A: Slow, deep breathing
options.B: Warm, flushed skin
options.C: High blood pressure
options.D: Fast heart rate

explanation: Tachycardia (fast heart rate) is the body's quick fix to keep blood moving when total volume starts to dip. You're mastering trauma basics!

question: How do second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics differ in receptor action from first-generation drugs?

options.A: They involve both dopamine and serotonin blockade
options.B: They only affect the endocrine system
options.C: They completely avoid binding to any dopamine receptors
options.D: They act exclusively as serotonin reuptake enhancers

explanation: Think of second-generation drugs as having a double action: they block both dopamine and serotonin receptors. This unique combination helps reduce side effects compared to older drugs.

question: How often should an emergency nurse reassess an unstable patient?

options.A: Only once at the very beginning of the shift
options.B: Only when the patient specifically asks for help
options.C: Continuously and frequently throughout the stay
options.D: Just before the patient is discharged home

explanation: Emergency conditions can change in a flash! Frequent, ongoing monitoring keeps you a step ahead.

question: How does acute physical or emotional stress falsely affect a Glucose Tolerance Test?

options.A: It destroys red blood cells and ruins the laboratory blood samples
options.B: It releases hormones like adrenaline and cortisol that raise blood sugar
options.C: It slows down digestion so the stomach cannot absorb the glucose drink
options.D: It forces the pancreas to release too much insulin, causing severe hypoglycemia

explanation: Stress hormones mobilize stored energy and push blood glucose levels up, which can mimic diabetes during the test. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h6)

question: Who is considered a 'stakeholder' in community health engagement?

options.A: Patient relatives who refuse to pay hospital admission bills
options.B: Anyone with an interest or role in the community's health
options.C: Only the medical doctors working in the federal teaching hospital
options.D: Foreign donors who live outside the African continent

explanation: Stakeholders include local chiefs, youth leaders, market women, and residents—anyone who cares about and is affected by the community's health.

question: Clearing stagnant water around houses to reduce mosquito breeding sites is an intervention aimed at which part of the epidemiological triangle?

options.A: Environment
options.B: Agent
options.C: Immunity
options.D: Host

explanation: Stagnant water is an environmental factor that supports vector breeding, so clearing it alters the environment to prevent disease. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T4#GNS225_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the main job of the government when working in partnership with NGOs?

options.A: Setting national policies and regulatory oversight
options.B: Manufacturing all global vaccines
options.C: Managing private donor bank accounts
options.D: Handling daily fundraising events abroad

explanation: That's correct! The government sets the rules, guidelines, and standards so that all health activities align nationally. [learn more](GNS124_U2_T6#GNS124_U2_T6_h4)

question: What do chemical indicator strips placed on a sterile pack actually tell the nurse?

options.A: The autoclave machine is fully repaired and working
options.B: The package was exposed to the required temperature or steam
options.C: The instruments inside have no rust or organic debris
options.D: All bacteria inside the pack are completely dead

explanation: Chemical indicators change color to show heat exposure, but they do not guarantee that the required time or conditions killed all germs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T68#GNS214_U1_T68_h4)

question: Which of these is a very common nursing diagnosis for a patient struggling with a severe phobia?

options.A: Impaired Gas Exchange
options.B: Deficient Fluid Volume
options.C: Risk for Infection
options.D: Ineffective Coping

explanation: Because phobias rely heavily on avoidance rather than healthy problem-solving, 'Ineffective Coping' fits right in your care plan.

question: When is the best time to check the second set of vital signs after starting a blood transfusion?

options.A: After thirty minutes
options.B: At the very end of the bag
options.C: After two hours
options.D: After fifteen minutes

explanation: The 15-minute mark is crucial because most serious acute reactions happen right at the beginning of the infusion.

question: What do the letters in the SBAR communication tool stand for?

options.A: System, Background, Action, Review
options.B: Symptoms, Behavior, Analysis, Response
options.C: Support, Briefing, Assessment, Recovery
options.D: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation

explanation: SBAR is a handy handover shortcut used by healthcare workers to share quick, important patient updates without missing a beat.

question: What is the core idea behind deductive reasoning?

options.A: Trusting a senior doctor purely because of their title
options.B: Moving from a general premise down to a specific conclusion
options.C: Accepting traditional habits without asking any questions
options.D: Gathering random facts until a pattern appears by chance

explanation: Deduction takes a known general rule and applies it to a specific situation to figure out what follows.

question: A patient with chronic bowel inflammation passes pale, bulky, foul-smelling stools that float. What nutritional problem does this suggest?

options.A: Fat malabsorption due to impaired intestinal function.
options.B: A sudden increase in stomach acid production.
options.C: Excessive intake of dietary fiber and green vegetables.
options.D: Rapid dehydration caused by drinking too little water.

explanation: Pale, bulky, and foul-smelling stools that float indicate steatorrhea, which means fats are not being absorbed properly in the gut. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T023#GNS227_U2_T023_h4)

question: Which specialist checks if a patient can swallow safely and recommends the right food textures?

options.A: Speech-language pathologist
options.B: Hospital pharmacist
options.C: Attending physician
options.D: Physical therapist

explanation: Correct! Speech therapists are experts at testing swallow safety and helping prevent dangerous choking or aspiration.

question: What is the tiny, functional building block of compact bone called?

options.A: Osteon
options.B: Trabecula
options.C: Periosteum
options.D: Epiphysis

explanation: An osteon is just the neat, cylinder-shaped repeating unit that makes up hard compact bone. Brilliant work!

question: Which high-touch surface in a patient room requires frequent routine disinfection?

options.A: Bedside tables and bed rails
options.B: The inside of closed closet drawers
options.C: Carpeted flooring under the bed
options.D: The ceiling tiles above the bed

explanation: High-touch items like bed rails and tables are frequently contaminated by hands and require regular cleaning. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which process is needed to completely destroy tough bacterial spores on surgical instruments?

options.A: Low-level disinfection
options.B: Wiping with clean water
options.C: Sterilization
options.D: Standard cleaning

explanation: Only full sterilization methods (like using an autoclave) are powerful enough to wipe out all germs and stubborn bacterial spores.

question: Why do nurses always encourage families to eat a variety of different foods?

options.A: Diversity in meals prevents food from spoiling in storage.
options.B: Eating only one type of food is the cheapest way to survive.
options.C: Eating a wide variety of foods ensures the body gets a complete range of essential nutrients.
options.D: Eating different foods eliminates the need for clean drinking water.

explanation: Brilliant! No single food item has every nutrient our bodies need, which is why a mixed diet is the secret to good health.

question: Why is it important to involve men and boys in community GBV prevention programs?

options.A: To replace international aid workers in distributing food supplies
options.B: To ensure they report all female community members to the police
options.C: To take over all nursing responsibilities inside the local clinic
options.D: To help shift patriarchal attitudes and challenge harmful cultural norms

explanation: Real prevention only happens when men and boys are part of the conversation, shifting old mindsets and helping stop violence at its root.

question: Which of these is a classic example of stopping a disease before it even starts (primary prevention)?

options.A: Treating complications of advanced diabetes
options.B: Screening adults for high blood pressure
options.C: Providing stroke rehabilitation exercises
options.D: Administering routine childhood immunizations

explanation: Spot on! Primary prevention stops illnesses before they happen. Vaccines are the ultimate example of keeping trouble away before it starts.

question: Why should a nurse worry if a patient completely cuts out a major food group?

options.A: It usually lacks essential nutrients required for normal bodily functions.
options.B: It permanently damages the digestive tract within twenty-four hours.
options.C: It always costs significantly more money than cooking regular meals.
options.D: It is strictly illegal under international public health laws.

explanation: Our bodies need a mix of everything—carbs, proteins, fats. Dropping a whole food group usually leads to vitamin shortages. Well spotted!

question: Why is epidemiological surveillance so important in community health?

options.A: To monitor disease trends and detect outbreaks early
options.B: To diagnose individual patients with chronic ailments
options.C: To design new pharmaceutical drugs in laboratories
options.D: To calculate monthly salaries for hospital staff members

explanation: You nailed it! Surveillance helps public health teams track disease patterns so they can catch and stop outbreaks early.

question: What is the biggest danger after a quality improvement project hits its initial goals?

options.A: The hospital running out of paper charts
options.B: Government regulators shutting down the unit
options.C: Patients refusing care from newly trained staff
options.D: Staff slowly slipping back into old, familiar habits over time

explanation: So true! Old habits die hard. Without active effort to keep new practices alive, teams easily slide right back into their old routines.

question: What happens when stool enters the rectum and you decide to hold it in for a bit?

options.A: The gut nerves completely reverse the direction of the waste.
options.B: The voluntary outer muscle contracts to override the reflex.
options.C: The parasympathetic nerves shut down all feeling completely.
options.D: The involuntary inner valve tightens up even more.

explanation: You consciously squeeze your skeletal external sphincter to keep things in check when it's not the right time or place to use the restroom. Perfectly normal!

question: Which of the following is NOT a true fact about modern post-abortion contraceptive use?

options.A: Ovulation returns within two weeks for many women after an abortion
options.B: Barrier methods protect against common sexually transmitted infections
options.C: Contraceptives cause permanent damage to a woman's reproductive organs
options.D: Intrauterine devices can be inserted safely right after a procedure

explanation: Standard reversible contraceptives do not cause permanent organ damage; fertility recovers once the method is stopped or removed. [learn more](GNS226_U5_T015#GNS226_U5_T015_h6)
